cards.front: How does machine learning differ from traditional programming?
cards.back: In traditional programming a person writes the **rules**, and the computer applies them to data. In machine learning the computer receives data and known answers and produces the rules itself.
cards.hint: Who writes the rules in each case?

cards.front: Why is some data kept back as testing data?
cards.back: So the model is judged on cases it never saw during training, giving an **honest** estimate of how it will perform on new data.
cards.hint: Think about a model that simply memorises its examples.

cards.front: Why does the quality of training data matter as well as the quantity?
cards.back: A model can only reflect patterns its data contains. Too few examples, or examples that miss common cases, give a **weak** model.
cards.hint: Could a very large dataset still miss common cases?

cards.front: What is a model in machine learning?
cards.back: A **model** is the set of rules or patterns produced by training, which is then used to make predictions on new data.

cards.front: What is the difference between a feature and a label?
cards.back: A **feature** is a measurable input property of an example. A **label** is the known correct output attached to a training example.
cards.hint: One goes in as input, the other is the known answer.

cards.back: **Overfitting** is when a model fits its training data so closely that it performs worse on new data.
cards.hint: Good on training data, poor on testing data.

cards.front: Does a machine learning model keep rewriting its own rules while it is being used?
cards.back: No. A model is usually **fixed** after training and then applied to new data. It does not normally rewrite itself.

cards.front: Name the five common kinds of task that machine learning solves.
cards.back: **Sorting** items into categories, **predicting** a number, **grouping** similar items, **recommending** items, and **spotting** unusual cases.
cards.hint: Think of spam filters and house prices.

cards.front: Which kind of task is image recognition, such as labelling a picture as cat or dog?
cards.back: **Sorting items into categories**. Each picture is assigned to a category.
cards.hint: Consider what the computer does with each picture.

cards.front: What are the steps of a machine learning workflow, in order?
cards.back: Define the problem and success measure, collect and prepare data, split into training and testing sets, train, evaluate on testing data, then **deploy** and monitor.
cards.hint: Start with deciding how success will be measured.

cards.front: A model scores 99% on its training data but only 60% on its testing data. What does this suggest?
cards.back: **Overfitting**. The model has learned quirks of its training examples rather than the general pattern.

cards.front: What should you do if the evaluation of a model is poor?
cards.back: You might **collect more data** or **change the model**, then repeat the earlier steps of the workflow.

cards.front: Why does monitoring continue after a model has been deployed?
cards.back: Accuracy can **fall** as real-world data changes, so the model must keep being checked on real data.
cards.hint: Think about what happens when the world changes.

cards.back: **Deployment** is the stage at which a trained model is put into real use to make predictions on new data.
